puerile

PYOOR-ul · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Puerile is childishly silly and trivial.

Their weekly food fight had gone from a fun tradition to a puerile mess that the dining hall staff refused to clean up twice.

Example

Instead of debating the actual policy, the two pundits spent their entire segment trading puerile jabs about each other's haircuts.

Trading childish insults instead of engaging with the real issue -- silly, trivial behavior beneath the occasion -- is a textbook example of something puerile.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

childish: Childish is the plain, everyday word for acting like a young child, and for actual children it is no insult at all -- a kindergartner's games are naturally childish. Puerile is never that neutral: it is a pointed put-down for behavior that falls beneath the age of the person doing it.

juvenile: Juvenile criticizes behavior for lacking the seriousness a situation calls for -- a juvenile prank during a fire drill. It is milder and more clinical than puerile, which adds open contempt: puerile behavior is not just unserious but embarrassingly beneath the adult doing it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

mature: sensible and grown-up in behavior

sophisticated: refined and intellectually advanced

Where it sits · how childish the foolishness is — silly → puerile → infantile

silly vs. puerile: Silly is far milder than puerile: silly fun is light and harmless -- a goofy hat, a made-up song -- and nobody is really being judged. Puerile behavior draws genuine scorn, because it sinks beneath the age of the person doing it.

infantile vs. puerile: Infantile is even stronger than puerile: puerile behavior is immature for a grown-up, while infantile behavior sinks all the way to a baby's level -- full tantrums, wailing, fists pounding the floor.

Build the Word

The pieces

origin — puer

origin — puer: boy, child (Latin)

suffix — -ile

suffix — -ile: of or like (as in juvenile) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Puerile comes from Latin puer, 'boy, child,' plus -ile, 'of or like,' as in juvenile -- so puerile literally means 'childlike,' behaving in a way that is silly, trivial, and beneath the seriousness the moment calls for.

Use the root in a new word: puericulture

Use the root in a new word: puericulture: Latin puer meant 'boy, child,' and puerile keeps the root's playground side. Puericulture, an old-fashioned term from about a hundred years ago, took the same root somewhere far more serious: doctors and nurses once studied it in medical school.

Word Choice

Puerile is a pointed insult aimed at adults (or adult behavior) that seems beneath their age -- contrast it with vapid, taught later in this unit, which criticizes something for being dull and empty rather than specifically childish.
